glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: Covering roughly 2026-09-07 to 2026-09-14: 69 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools and the week's arguments. This tab is the week in one screen; each section has its own tab with its items in full, the checks against their sources and what happened next.
glance.theme: The week's theme: agents became the unit everything is built, sold and measured around. DeepSeek reshaped V4.1-Flash for the prompt and cache costs of long agent loops; OpenAI and Anthropic now run the loop itself as a product; the week's benchmarks scored the agent with its harness attached, so the same model reads 62.7% or 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3; and Anthropic's threat report and the Claude Mythos 5 incident showed agents doing the attacking, which is the backdrop to Dario Amodei's call to pace the frontier. The [[animation in Top stories|t-top|v-ced]] runs one agent turn through DeepSeek's old and new architectures.
glance.next_title: What happened next, in one line each (as of 2026-10-02)

sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Amodei's call to pace the frontier; DeepSeek's encoder-decoder (animated); the agent loop as a product; Real-SWE on private code (three readings); AI-run cyber operations.
sections.lead: Five stories with one subject: agents. DeepSeek changed the shape of a model so that long agent loops cost less to serve, and the animation below runs one agent turn through the new architecture and the decoder-only one it replaces. OpenAI and Anthropic now run the agent loop as a hosted service with a control surface, and Sakana sells an orchestrator as if it were a model. Real-SWE measured agents on private company code, then rewrote its own table twice after the issue went out; the card below shows all three readings. Anthropic's threat report documents agents running real intrusions. And Dario Amodei, citing the agent incidents of the summer, asked the industry to slow capability gains and committed Anthropic to embedded outside evaluators.

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: An orchestrator sold as a model (Sakana Fugu); a coding agent on Kimi K3 (Cognition SWE-2); a translation-only MoE; voice, image, music and on-device releases; Meta's agent in a VM.
sections.lead: Thirteen releases, and few of them are plain models. The biggest, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, is told in [[Top stories|t-top|i-deepseek-v41]]. Sakana's Fugu is an orchestrator that routes each request across a pool of other models behind one API; Cognition's SWE-2 is Moonshot's open Kimi K3 post-trained into a coding agent that only runs inside Devin; Cohere's North Small Translate is a 218B mixture of experts that does one job. The rest is the interface layer: full-duplex voice, images, licensed music, small on-device and vision models, a document parser, and two assistants, Meta's Muse agent, which runs each instance in its own virtual machine, and Gemini on Windows. Several headline numbers are the vendors' own measurements; the checks under each item say which.

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: Agents as insiders (MOLE); scores that depend on the harness; the Recurrent Looped Transformer (animated); pretraining gains from data; Anthropic's 2030 scenarios (calculator).
sections.lead: Thirteen items in four threads. Agents as insiders: MOLE finds that most agent models complete harmful objectives inside an organisation and the best monitors miss nearly half of it, and NeoHorse-1 feeds a serving harness back into training. The harness as part of the result: Hyper-tau-bench (23.9% alone, 82.2% with an engineer), ARC-AGI-3 at 62.7% or 99.9% depending on the harness, and Phi-Bench on infrastructure engineering; Real-SWE lives in [[Top stories|t-top|v-rswe]]. Architecture and training: the Recurrent Looped Transformer, which carries the decoder's state from token to token (animated below against a standard decoder, and the opposite trade to DeepSeek's encoder-decoder in [[Top stories|t-top|v-ced]]), Magic's and Dwarkesh's pretraining-efficiency results, and Random Attention. Then two claims about the world outside the lab: OpenAI's Navier-Stokes result and Anthropic's economic scenarios, whose central number the calculator below multiplies out.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO against Altman's no-IPO; SoftBank's loan for OpenAI; Mistral's 3 billion euros; a $13.7B GPU deal; safety researchers moving to METR; Pentagon contracts; chip and robotics rounds; AI harms.
sections.lead: Fourteen items, most of them money or people. The two frontier labs split on going public: Anthropic chose Nasdaq for October and guided to a second profitable quarter, while Sam Altman ruled out an OpenAI listing this year, citing safety, and SoftBank borrowed $11.87 billion to keep funding OpenAI. Mistral raised the largest round in European tech; Anthropic added a $13.7 billion GPU contract; Positron and Ayar Labs raised for inference chips and optical links (Positron's bet is explained in [[Compute|t-compute|i-positron-hbm]]). The people story is safety researchers leaving labs for the evaluator METR in the same week Amodei proposed embedding evaluators like METR inside labs ([[Top stories|t-top|i-pacing]]). The rest is policy and harm: Pentagon agreements, a California law on chatbots and minors, licensed fan remixes, AI-made abuse imagery in Meta's ads and an invoice-fraud campaign.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: Positron's bet against HBM; TPUv7 Ironwood sold outside Google; Arm's N4; ROCm 10 with agent skills; Cerebras at up to 1,850 tokens per second; China's 2030 target; power for data centres; a 2nm phone chip.
sections.lead: Eight items about where inference will run and what limits it. The chip stories split on memory: Positron is designing around commodity LPDDR5X instead of HBM, betting that capacity per dollar matters more than peak bandwidth, while Google's TPUv7 Ironwood is now sold for other companies' inference at up to 50% better performance per dollar than Nvidia's B200 and B300, per SemiAnalysis. Why bandwidth sets the ceiling for a single stream of tokens is worked out in [[Dev tools|t-dev|v-sol]]; Cerebras's 1,500 to 1,850 tokens per second on Qwen3.8-27B is what wafer-scale on-chip memory buys. AMD shipped its optimisation know-how as agent skills. The rest is capacity and power: China's 2030 target, Australian and Iowa power deals, a Massachusetts rule that large data centres pay for their own clean energy, and a phone chip that doubles on-device AI throughput.

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: The agent loop hosted (OpenAI) and governed (Anthropic); Cohere's megakernel serving engine (speed-of-light calculator); Claude Code and Codex releases; coordinator agents; an agent inbox; a DeepSeek sandbox CVE.
sections.lead: Ten items. The first two are one story, told in [[Top stories|t-top|i-harness-buy]]: OpenAI now runs the agent loop for you, and Anthropic lets your server approve or block each step of its managed agents. Cohere's account of a decode megakernel inside a complete serving engine is the week's best systems read; the calculator below reproduces its speed-of-light arithmetic and shows why a long context eats into it. Then the tools: Claude Code 2.1.266 to 2.1.270, Codex 0.154.0, Cursor's coordinator agent, AWS's inbox for background agents, Deep Research inside OpenAI's work apps, and a sandbox escape in DeepSeek's agent tooling. The last item says several release feeds were quiet; GitHub's records say otherwise.

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk of the town
sections.glance: A mathematicians' declaration against AI's race for famous problems; a rejoinder to the pacing debate; Bengio on agents that lie and coordinate; Nvidia as a central bank; what drew attention and what did not.
sections.lead: Six threads from Hacker News and the essays people argued over. The biggest was a declaration by mathematicians that AI companies' race to solve famous problems works against the way mathematics actually advances, published as OpenAI claimed a Navier-Stokes result ([[Research|t-research|i-navier]]). Two pieces answered the pacing debate from opposite sides: "Everyone should slow down AI development except for me" and Yoshua Bengio on why agents lie, cheat and coordinate. The Economist cast Nvidia as the AI economy's central bank. And the attention itself was data: Amodei's 6-to-12-month warning drew 46 points, David Sacks's case against regulation 221.

followups.t: DeepSeek kept V4 Pro after all
followups.html: By the changelog's capture of 13 September the routing plan was gone, replaced by: "In response to user demand, we have decided to continue providing API services for DeepSeek V4 Pro after September 14, 2026, with the billing method remaining unchanged" ({{archived 13 Sep|https://web.archive.org/web/20260913121105/https://api-docs.deepseek.com/updates/}}). On 2 October the pricing page still lists deepseek-v4-pro (DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813) at $1.32 and $3.96 per million at peak; only the old Flash names route to V4.1-Flash ({{pricing|https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing}}). The technical report followed on 17 September and confirms the cache figures animated above ({{arXiv 2609.19969|https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19969}}), and vLLM v0.30.0 added V4.1-Flash on 22 September ({{release notes|https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.30.0}}).

By 15 September Grok 4.6 had been re-run: 23.8% became 32.5%, third place, at $2.67 a rollout instead of $3.44, with every other cell unchanged ({{archived 15 Sep|https://web.archive.org/web/20260915063330/https://withspecific.com/benchmarks/real-swe}}). By 28 September every model had been re-scored on two tasks (Billing schedule migration from 9 passes in 64 to 50, API token metering from 8 to 14): GPT-6 Astra now leads at 46.25% ahead of Fable 5.1 at 45.00%, only four tasks stay below 15%, and the short-rollout failure rate reads 57.4% against 66.2% for longer ones ({{live page|https://withspecific.com/benchmarks/real-swe}}). No change note was published. The card above shows all three readings.

The project page, updated 20 September with two co-authors (Jichen Feng, Shihan Qin), now reports trained models: eight-layer encoder-decoder splits against an eight-layer Transformer on six algorithmic tasks, three seeds each (a 17 September snapshot). Several splits learn parity earlier and keep 100% at 256 bits; on swaps-based permutation tracking at length 512 the 4+4 split reaches 55.70% against 0.85% for the Transformer; addition beyond trained widths and standard permutation tracking stay hard. The 48 + 48 tied layout remains an illustration; the experiments use untied 8- and 16-layer models of 25 to 29 million parameters ({{project page|https://yifanzhang-pro.github.io/recurrent-looped-tranformer/}}).

followups.t: Anthropic's first release tested by outside evaluators
followups.html: On 18 September Anthropic published the measurements behind the essay: more than 80% of code merged into its codebase authored by Claude as of May 2026 and the typical engineer merging 8 times as much code per day as in 2024, with its own caveat that lines of code overstate the gain ({{Anthropic, recursive self-improvement|https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement}}). On 22 September it released Claude Opus 5.5, "our first release since we called for pacing the frontier", which it says "was tested before release by external evaluators, including Frontier Design and METR" ({{Anthropic|https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-5-5}}).

followups.t: Court upholds the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic
followups.html: A federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. upheld the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk, rejecting the company's challenge ({{CNBC|https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/25/pentagon-anthropic-ai-risk-appeals-court.html}}).

vLLM shipped v0.30.0 on 22 September, thirteen days after v0.29.0, with Fast Start (weights kept in GPU memory across engine restarts), output watermarking and support for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, among much else ({{release notes|https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases/tag/v0.30.0}}, {{release list|https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/releases}}).

followups.t: Scientific American: did OpenAI solve the wrong problem?
followups.html: Scientific American argues that OpenAI used the Clay problem's option that allows an external force, which most mathematicians regard as the less natural version, quoting Luis Silvestre: "The Clay problem is settled, but the main problem for the Navier-Stokes equations is not"; three mathematicians have posted a proof that the forced method cannot extend to the unforced problem ({{Scientific American|https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/did-openai-solve-the-wrong-navier-stokes-problem/}}). The Clay Institute has not accepted the claim, and the paper is not peer reviewed ({{Implicator|https://www.implicator.ai/clay-institute-navier-stokes-openai-proof-claim/}}).
